_comment: C0-5 body translation for coding/grok-bot. Keys align with build.mjs: axes by axis key; sections/sectionTitles by the Chinese section headings of extraSections; runs/unknowns/related/sources by index alignment with the Chinese side.
_rules: 0) Keep ** emphasis, `code`, links and table structure, block-for-block with the Chinese side.
1) Official English quotes stay verbatim; Chinese-rendered paraphrases of official wording are marked (translated) on the English side — never fabricate English originals.
2) Do not upgrade 'unverified / not stated officially' semantics; the translation changes no facts.

axes.model_access:
**The official pages name no underlying model and never say whether the model can be swapped.**

(x.ai's "Introducing Grok Bot" and "Grok Bot is now included with more plans" pages both checked.)

Parallel in-site evidence: the same-period **Introducing Grok 4.6** page writes:

**Official wording**: "a particular focus on long-running agents"

This matches Grok Bot's always-on positioning.

**But the two pages never name each other.**

So this site does not write "Grok Bot runs on 4.6" (R5: no inference).

Compared with the other two:

- OpenAI Dot — explicitly names GPT‑6 Astra
- Meta Muse — explicitly names Muse Spark
- Grok Bot — blank

**Whether the model can be swapped, and to which ones, is not stated officially.**
axes.runtime:
**The form factor is isomorphic with the other two: its own cloud computer, always on.**

Official wording:

They have their own computer, work inside tools and apps like you do, and keep working 24/7

Another post writes:

They have their own computer in the cloud. It's always on, with browser and terminal access

**Having a terminal is one distinguishable difference between this entry and the other two.**

The official wording says browser **and terminal** access, while both Dot and Muse officially mention only the browser.

The difference the official pages stress is "work happens in the actual tool instead of a chat draft":

They sign into your apps and work happens in the actual tool instead of a chat draft

Available surfaces: official wording says desktop and iOS.
axes.local_files:
**The official pages never mention the local file system; its workspace is its own cloud machine.**

The official wording uses single quotes, citing the same sentence as elsewhere:

They have their own computer. It's always on, with browser and terminal access

The workspace visible indirectly is the signed-in apps — official examples include audit email, Drive, and paid subscriptions, plus:

Works across apps and inboxes

That shows it really does touch mail and cloud drive.

**Permission granularity and whether there is full sync are not stated officially.**

(Two launch pages and the x.ai/bot governance spec checked.)
axes.background:
**The official pages give a duration promise directly: 24/7.**

Launch page wording:

keep working 24/7

Another post's wording:

Bots work across apps and inboxes, keep going when you step away, and only pull you in for judgment calls

**The clearest sentence in this dimension is "only pull you in for judgment calls".**

It pins the callback condition to "when judgment is needed", not periodic reporting.

There is also an official hardening mechanism:

Ask a Bot to follow along the next time you do the job, so it can run on its own after that

i.e. teach it once, then it runs by itself.

And it is explicitly parallelizable:

Stand up a researcher, writer, and chief of staff. Put them in a group chat so they pass work between themselves

**The permission level of tools during autonomous background work (read-only or read-write) is not stated officially.**

(Two launch pages and the x.ai/bot governance spec checked — the latter only lists must-approve actions, not permission levels.)
axes.tools:
**The official pages replace a capability table with a list of "routine jobs", and that list is itself the selection basis.**

The jobs listed in official wording:

Bots doing today

The list (nine roles):

- Sales prospector — sales leads
- Website builder — site building
- Digital declutterer — digital cleanup
- Customer support — support
- Game artist — game art
- Office manager — office scheduling
- Inbox manager — inbox
- Meeting stand-in — meeting proxy
- Refunds manager — refund chasing

Specific external services named officially: payments provider, Gmail, Slack, ServiceTitan, Quo, client portal, Drive. (named officially)

**It is the only one of the three that never mentions payment checkout — the official Grok Bot launch page does not say it can check out directly.**

Meta Muse explicitly names Stripe Link; Dot does not mention it. **This site does not infer; it only records that the official pages do not mention it.**

The "Website builder" entry officially writes purchases the domain and deploys the final version — **procurement is involved**, and approval ownership is not separately stated.
axes.context:
**The official framing is interaction memory, not context window.**

Official wording:

They remember conversations, learn how you like things done, and get sharper the more work together

The entry point is a single text thread:

A text-thread UX. Message a Bot the way you would message someone on your team, from mobile or desktop, so you can pick up the same thread on either — with nothing to set up first

**i.e. the same conversation thread continues across devices.**

Multi-Bot collaboration has its own description: they pass work to each other in a group chat, with the user not in the middle.

**Context-window size, and how memory is stored and deleted, are not stated officially.**

(Two launch pages and the x.ai/bot governance spec checked. By contrast Meta Muse officially provides deletion and a forget skill — this is a conspicuous information gap in this entry.)
axes.permissions:
**Only one approval layer is written on the launch pages: "callback equals approval". A Bot governance spec on the official domain adds the must-approve action list.**

Verification supplemented 2026-10-03; the nature of that spec is discussed in the body section "How to read that governance spec".

Three points verified on the launch pages:

1. Callback equals approval — "only come back when something needs your approval",
   "Leaves every send for you to approve in your inbox or navigator"
2. Routine jobs carry conservative verbs — declutterer "Only discards or unsubscribes if
   you say so"; refunds manager "Comes back with the refund or discount it
   recovered" — it does not execute refunds itself, it brings the result back
3. One design worth noting — Website builder officially writes
   "Helps configure plugins, delivers a live URL, and adds redirect rules",
   **it even changes DNS redirects, yet the official site does not list it as an approval-required item**

**The Bot governance spec on the official domain `x.ai/bot/…` gives an explicit approval list.**

Original prefix:

Explicit approval required before…

Must-approve actions:

- Creating / editing / duplicating / hiding / deleting a Bot
- Saving or materially modifying a Skill
- Creating / enabling / editing / pausing a Routine
- Creating or changing group chats
- Installing or authenticating connectors
- **Expanding permissions**
- Writing to external sources
- Sending or publishing
- Contacting external people
- **Purchases, transfers, price changes, commercial commitments**
- Deleting or overwriting data
- Changing production environments
- Accepting legal terms
- Sensitive hiring / medical / legal / financial decisions
- Creating public share links or marketplace submissions

Three behavioral rules directly relevant to this dossier:

1. Silence is not consent — official wording "**Do not infer approval from silence, vague
   agreement, a previous approval, another version, or an example**"
2. Approval does not spill over — official wording "Approval applies only to the **exact action,
   target, scope, version, configuration, connection, permission, and
   schedule**"
3. Deletion requires a human — official wording "**Never delete a Bot automatically**"
   plus "Agents cannot be deleted by another agent; **the user deletes from the
   sidebar**"

There are also two credential rules:

**Never store credentials**

Never request passwords, passkeys, 2FA, private keys, recovery codes, payment confirmations, or API secrets in chat

**Product-level mechanisms are not stated officially.**

Four things the official pages do not state.

A customizable permission-rule UI, an auto-reviewer, audit logs. And the technical custody method for credentials.

One more unstated item: whether that spec is product-level enforcement or a constraint on individual Bots.

What was found is a Bot behavior spec, not a product-mechanism document.

(Two launch pages and the x.ai/bot spec checked.)
axes.fit:
**Fits people who pick agents by job role.**

The official pages give a role-based jobs list (see the tools axis), usable as a checklist: sales leads, site building, inbox cleanup, customer support, game art, office scheduling, inbox, meeting stand-in, refund chasing.

**Does not fit four kinds of people:**

- People who need the permission mechanism inspectable and configurable — this entry's most obvious shortcoming
- People who need local file read/write
- People who need the underlying model confirmed — not published officially
- Users outside English-speaking regions — official wording covers only desktop and iOS; **the regional statement goes only to surfaces, with no country list**

sections.三份里只有本条查不到审批机制:
This is the single most important thing this dossier should say up front.

The three vendors' mechanism comparison:

| | OpenAI Dot | Meta Muse | **Grok Bot** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Approval mechanism | Auto-review + custom rules + **sensitive actions always human** | **Independent Sentinel agent**, system-level isolation | **Not described on the launch pages**; the in-domain Bot spec lists must-approve actions |
| Credentials | Uses stored passwords without exposing them to the model | Secure Credentials Store | **Not described on the launch pages**; the spec only says "Never store credentials" |
| Audit | Activity view | Full trace, including "plans to do" | **Not described on the launch pages** |

**The "callback equals approval" layer is verified:**

> only come back when something needs your approval
>
> Leaves every send for you to approve in your inbox or navigator

**Supplemented 2026-10-03: the in-domain Bot behavior spec adds approval granularity (which actions require approval).**

But it does **not** add "whether users can configure their own rules", "audit logs", or "how credentials are kept".

So the last two rows of the table above still read "not described on the launch pages", and that is accurate.

**The selection implication still holds, but the reason changes.**

If "is the approval mechanism inspectable and configurable" is a hard requirement, this entry **still cannot be answered completely from official material** — what was found is a Bot behavior spec, not a product-mechanism document.

For an answer you must ask xAI; do not assume "it should be there".
sections.那份治理规范怎么读（重要，别当成产品机制）:
There is a public Bot behavior spec on the `x.ai` domain (`x.ai/bot/…`) containing a fairly complete approval list.

**It fills the approval granularity missing from the launch pages, but its nature must be made clear.**

| | Content |
|---|---|
| What it **is** | A **behavioral-constraint statement** for one Bot — how it should act, what it should ask first |
| What it ❌ **is not** | Not product documentation; not a product-level permission-mechanism statement; it does not mean all Bots are bound by the same ruleset; it cannot answer "can rules be configured in the user UI" |

**Why this distinction matters:**

It tells you "**how this Bot is required to behave**",
not "**what this product lets you configure**".

What users really want to know is "can I decide myself which actions need approval" —
**this document does not answer that question**, so `permissions` still cannot count as filled.

**But two of its designs deserve separate note**, and they form interesting contrasts with the other two vendors:

1. **"Do not infer approval from silence"** —
   silence is not consent. This is stricter than Dot's two tiers of "Ask for some actions / Always ask":
   **xAI explicitly forbids inferring consent from "not objecting", at the spec level.**
2. **"Approval applies only to the exact action, target, scope, version,
   configuration, connection, permission, and schedule"** —
   **approval is pinned to the single action and single configuration; it does not spill into the next time.**
   This contrasts with Muse's granularity options:

   - Allow once / for this task / for this site / Always allow

   These are two different granularity philosophies: Muse offers
   **validity-duration options**, while this Grok Bot spec
   recognizes **one-time approval only**.

**Three-vendor approval model comparison (after the supplement)**

| | Approval granularity | Does silence count as consent | Duration options |
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenAI Dot | Custom rules + built-in floor + auto-review | No statement seen | No statement seen |
| Meta Muse | Five-tier options | No statement seen | Yes (once / task / site / always) |
| **Grok Bot** | **Spec lists must-approve actions** | **Explicitly not** | **Single-use approval only** |
sections.两处值得单独记的细节:
### ① Routine jobs use conservative verbs

Official wording:

```
Digital declutterer — Audits email, Drive, and paid subscriptions around the clock.
Only discards or unsubscribes if you say so.

Refunds manager — Finds the claim, files it, and follows it through.
Comes back with the refund or discount it recovered.
```

The declutterer **audits continuously but discards only if you say so**.
The refunds manager **runs the whole process but brings the result back to you**.

**In the official descriptions none of these jobs "execute on its own"** —
this is the behavioral boundary as presented by the official page text, not speculation.

### ② But the Website builder entry does both purchasing and deploying

Official wording:

```
Website builder — Builds the site, purchases the domain, and deploys
the final version. Helps configure plugins, delivers a live URL,
and adds redirect rules.
```

**Buying the domain + going live + changing redirects are all done, and the official site does not list it as an approval-required item.**

This is inconsistent with the conservative wording of ①.

**This site records the inconsistency as-is** — no cover-up for the vendor,
and no verdict that an approval is missing either (approval may live in the product rather than on the launch page).
sections.底层模型：官方没点名，本档案不推断:
- OpenAI Dot: explicitly GPT‑6 Astra
- Meta Muse: explicitly Muse Spark
- **Grok Bot: the official pages give no model name**

In-site one can see the Grok 4.6 launch page writing "a particular focus on long-running agents",
and Grok Bot is exactly the always-on type — **but the two pages never name each other.**

So this site does not write "Grok Bot runs on 4.6".

**Reason**: the v3 rule "give the basis for judgment, not false conclusions" —
"two products' positioning matches" is not evidence for "the same model".
sections.计费：与另两家是不同的结构:
**This official statement is repeated on both official pages — a point the vendor stresses.**

> Grok Bot comes with its own usage, separate from your Grok and Cursor plans,
> so anything you hand off to a Bot won't count against your existing usage.

The three vendors' structures compared:

| | Dot | Muse | Grok Bot |
|---|---|---|---|
| What you buy | Bundled with Pro / Business Premium | Most needs free + subscription tiers | Bundled with SuperGrok / Cursor tiers |
| Relation to main-plan quota | Dot chats don't count; tasks handed to Codex **do count** | Not stated officially | **Independent usage, separate from the main plan** |

**The three use three different structures — do not assume "vendor-cloud agents are all the same".**

⚠ **The concrete numbers for the independent usage are given by neither official page**; check the official site yourself.

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs. The test protocol is at [protocols/coding/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/coding/_protocol.md).

**Suggested measurement**: if you can subscribe to any SuperGrok or Cursor tier,
the single most valuable thing to test in this entry is the **approval trigger point**.

The official pages only say "needs your approval",
so whether "Website builder buying a domain" actually pops an approval prompt is the only way to fill this gap.

**Do not test benchmarks**: like the other two it installs nothing locally, so there is no local benchmark to run.
unknowns:
- **Which underlying model** — not named officially
- **Whether there is an auto-reviewer** — Dot has one; Grok Bot's launch pages do not describe it
- **How credentials are kept** — only the spec's "Never store credentials" is known; the technical method is unstated
- **Whether there is a customizable permission-rule UI** — the spec gives a list but does not say users can configure their own
- **Whether there are audit logs** — not described officially
- Whether that Bot behavior spec is product-level enforcement or a per-Bot constraint — the document does not state its scope
- Concrete numbers for the independent usage
- Existence and boundary of a free tier — the official pages only say it is billed separately from the main plan, not whether it can be used free
- Regional availability — official wording covers surfaces only, no country list
- The permission level of tools during autonomous background work (read-only or read-write)
